newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Ukraine say Black Sea fleet row resolved.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Ukraine say Black Sea fleet row resolved.

text.p: The prime ministers of Russia and Ukraine said they had settled a protracted dispute over a shareout of the former Soviet Black Sea fleet on Wednesday by leasing its naval base at Sevastopol to Russia for 20 years.

Russia's Viktor Chernomyrdin and Ukraine's Pavlo Lazarenko signed the deal and a series of other documents and told reporters they had opened the way for a long-delayed visit to Kiev by Russian President Boris Yeltsin later this week.
Yeltsin is expected to crown a long-delayed trip to Ukraine on Friday and Saturday with a friendship treaty outlining long-term relations between the two Slav neighbours.

"We have prepared the ground for President Yeltsin's visit and for the summit talks," said Chernomyrdin, who held three hours of tense talks with Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma earlier on Wednesday.
"We are opening a new page in the history of relations between our people," he added.

Chernomyrdin and Lazarenko signed three documents tackling the status of the Russian part of the fleet which will be based in Sevastopol on the Crimean peninsula, financial terms of the lease and criteria for the final shareout of the fleet.
In theory such agreements need parliamentary ratification but neither Chernomyrdin nor Lazarenko referred to this. Officials were not immediately available for comment.

Both men declined to reveal financial details of the lease and it was clear the issue of extending the 20-year term had not been agreed. "The issue of prolonging the lease was not discussed today. Let's take time and see," Lazarenko said. "At least for the first 20 years," Chernomyrdin added.
Russia and Ukraine have announced more than once in the past they had reached a final deal on the fleet but many of their earlier commitments sank amid mutual mistrust and recrimination.
Chernomyrdin said the two countries had no outstanding problems in this area and that they would concentrate on carrying out Wednesday's decisions.

Georgia, another former Soviet republic on the Black Sea, restated its claim to part of the fleet on Wednesday when President Eduard Shevardnadze said Tbilisi wanted some warships which had been based at the Georgian port of Poti until 1992.

Russia's Itar-Tass news agency quoted Shevardnadze as saying he had sent two written messages to Yeltsin recently, calling his attention to Georgia's desire for part of the Black Sea Fleet, but had not received any reply.
In Kiev, Chernomyrdin and Kuchma took up another sensitive issue in bilateral relations, signing several economic agreements aimed at boosting trade.
"The sides have voiced concern over a dramatic decline in trade turnover and decided to lift all barriers which stand in the way of bilateral trade," Kuchma's spokesman Dmytro Markov told reporters.
He gave no details, but Kiev has complained about what it saw as discriminatory Russian policies while Moscow accused Ukraine of dumping cheap and poor quality goods on its market.
Yeltsin had cancelled six visits to sign the friendship treaty but with Moscow busy shaping new relations with the West, settling old grievances with Ukraine is in the Kremlin's interest.

Yeltsin and leaders of NATO countries signed a historic pact on Tuesday under which Moscow acquired some say in the Western defence alliance in exchange for acceptance of its plans to admit several eastern European countries.

The Kremlin, which had hailed the deal with NATO as an end to confrontation in Europe, is nevertheless worried by prospects of any further advance eastwards by NATO to countries which once were part of the Soviet Union.

Russian officials have said Moscow wanted to encourage Ukraine to stick to plans to sign a special deal with NATO rather then seek membership in the alliance like the three Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
